paragraphs: Tzarik lehizzaher meod bekibbud ab vaem umoraam v"p sheen bet din kopin al mitzva dekol mitzva asher mattan sekarah betziddah en bet din kopin aleha mikkol maqom im ratzu likpot hareshut beyadam ella sheen kopin kepiyya ad shettetze napsho veayyen t"z verishon letziyyon za"l vekol zeh davqa al meniat hakkabod abal al zilzul im mezalzel bahem chayyabim likpoto middina veayyen keneset haggedola haggahat hattur ot ':

clarification.explanation: One must be very careful with the commandments of honoring and revering one's father and mother. Although a court does not forcibly compel fulfillment of a commandment whose reward is written alongside it (like honoring parents), if the court wishes to compel it, they have the authority to do so, except they do not use harsh compulsion to the point of endangering life. All this concerns one who refrains from honoring his parents, but one who actively disrespects and demeans them — the court must compel him by strict law.
takeaways: Honoring and revering parents is an obligation requiring great care.
For mere failure to honor, no harsh compulsion is used, but the court has authority to compel.
For actively demeaning parents, the court must compel by strict law.

paragraphs: Ezehu mora lo yaamod bammaqom hamyuchad laamod sham besod zeqenim im chabero o maqom hamyuchad lo lehitpallel velo yesheb bammaqom hamyuchad lo lehaseb bo bebeto abal muttar laamod bemaqom sheabiv ragil lesheb bebeto vekol zeh hu davqa bepanayv vaapillu shello bepinu im hayu bene adam yoshebim sham vehu ba veyesheb bimqom abiv gam ken asur dehave zilluta veyesh machmirim leesor apillu shello bipne abiv velo bipne acherim ella raq bipne atzmo bilbad vetzarik lachush ledibrehem kevan dezeh hu issur tora veayyen t"z verishon letziyyon:

clarification.explanation: "Fear of one's father": one should not stand in the place designated for his father to stand among his peers in the council of elders, or in the place designated for him to pray; and should not sit in the place designated for his father to recline in his home. But it is permitted to stand in the place his father normally sits plainly at home. All this applies specifically in his presence; and even not in his presence, if people were sitting there and he comes and sits in his father's place — it is forbidden (being disrespectful). Some are stricter, forbidding this even not in his father's presence and not in others' presence, but alone by himself — and one should be concerned for their view, since this is a Torah-level prohibition (Taz, Rishon LeTzion).
takeaways: Fear of a father: do not stand/sit in his designated place (among elders, in prayer, or reclining at home) — but a place he sits plainly is permitted.
Forbidden in his presence; also not in his presence if others are sitting there (disrespect); some are stricter even alone — proper to be concerned (Torah-level prohibition).

paragraphs: Lo yakria et debarayv bepanayv apillu lomar "nirin dibre abba" vekol shekken shello yistor debarayv bepanayv ben shecholeq alayv ben sheomer leadam hacholeq alayv nirin debareka abal shello bepanayv shari umikkol maqom, kol mah sheepshar laasot derek kabod oseh dehaynu im hu choleq al dibre abiv veyesh chakam echad gam ken choleq - hu yokicha veyiktob dato kedaat hacholeq al abiv abal lo yazkir shem abiv vekayyotze bazeh veyesh machmirin veoserin besoter debarayv apillu shello bepanayv umikkol maqom lekulle alema habben im haab yekolim lehaqshot uletaretz ulehassiq masqenat hahalaka veen bazeh chashash mishshum soter debarayv veayyen pitche teshuba seip qatan ';

clarification.explanation: A son should not decide or rule between his father's words in his presence, even to say in a supportive tone that his father's words seem correct, and all the more so should not contradict his father's words in his presence, whether he disagrees himself or tells another person who disagrees with his father that his words seem correct. But not in his father's presence, it is permitted. Nevertheless he should act respectfully: if he disagrees with his father and there is another scholar who also disagrees, he should attribute his view to the other scholar and not mention his father's name. Some are stricter, forbidding contradicting the father's words even not in his presence. But according to all opinions, it is permitted for father and son together to raise questions, answer them, and clarify the halacha, with no concern of contradicting the father's words.
takeaways: One should not decide or contradict a father's words in his presence, even in a supportive tone.
Not in his presence it is permitted, though it is proper to attribute a disagreeing view to another scholar.
Joint study of questions and answers to clarify halacha is permitted according to all opinions.

paragraphs: Lo yiqraennu bishmo lo bechayyayv velo bemoto ella omer abba mari peloni o mor abi peloni haya shem abiv keshem acherim meshanneh shemam im hu shem pile sheen hakkol regilin liqrot bo abal shem shergilin liqrot muttar liqrot laacherim shello bepanayv v"g deyesh mattirin liqrot acherim beshem sheeno pile apillu bepanayv veken od yesh mattirim liqro laacherim beshem pile shello bepanayv hinneh ledidan sheqqibbalnu horaat maran za"l tzarik lizzaher bazeh mihu muttar liqrot battana"k ubedibre rz"l lipne abiv v"p shennizkar bahem shem abiv v"p shehu shem peliy kevan shehu mazkiro bedibre tora venikkar name deeno qore et abiv atzmo abal lo yiqra miktab meadam lachabero shennizkar bo shem adam sheshshemo keshem abiv im hu shem peliy vezeh davqa bepanayv abal shello bepanayv im nikkar mittok haddebarim delav al abiv medabber shari "p shehu shem peliy vekaasher haaleti ken bsh"q mqbtzyl bs"d veod haaleti sham daapillu beshem pile im abiv shemo naptali veen lo kinnuy mishpacha vehu mazkir lipne abiv shem naptali lureya o im haya abiv separaddi vehu mazkir lipne abiv naptali ashkenazzi vegam od mukach mittok debarayv shehu medabber al adam acher kegon sheomer leabiv naptali ashkenazzi omer o halak o katabti lo o katab li vekayyotze bazeh shennikkar mittok debarayv delav al abiv hu medabber let lan bah "p shehu shem peliy umazkiro bepanayv kevan deikka tarte limalyuta sheyyesh shinnuy beshem atzmo vegam nikkar mittok haddebarim delav al abiv hu medabber umazkir: ubachatima muttar lachtom yitzchaq ben abraham deen ketiba chashiba kedibbur leinyan zeh veyesh mitchassedim liktob yitzchaq ben laadoni abi abraham veen bazeh chiyyub min haddin v"g dekatabnu deen ketiba chashiba kedibbur leinyan zeh mikkol maqom im hu koteb ketab leabiv tzarik sheyyiktob lo mor abi o abba mari peloni veken beshekkoteb miktab laacherim umazkir bo shem abiv gam ken yiktob mor abi peloni veken hu haddin keshekkoteb shem abiv bepinqas shello becheshbonot vekayyotze gam ken yiktob mor abi vedin zeh shel hazkarat hashshem noheg gam beimmo shetztzarik lizzaher bekol hannizkar leel:

clarification.explanation: A son should not call his father by his first name, neither during his life nor after his death, but should say "my father, my teacher, so-and-so" or "my honored father so-and-so." If his father's name is the same as other people's and he needs to mention those people, he should slightly alter their name if it is a rare, uncommon name, but a common name may be mentioned regarding others not in his father's presence. Following Maran's ruling we have accepted, one should be careful about this. It is permitted to read Scripture and the words of the Sages before his father even if his father's name is mentioned in them, since it is clear he is reading words of Torah and not calling his father. If it is clear from the context that the father is not meant, it is permitted to mention the name, especially when there is a change in the name itself and it is also clear the father is not intended. In signing a letter, it is permitted to sign "Isaac son of Abraham," since writing is not considered speech for this purpose, and some are meticulous to write "Isaac son of my lord, my father, Abraham." But when writing a letter to his father or mentioning his father's name in a letter or a register entry, he should write "my honored father so-and-so." This law applies to one's mother as well.
takeaways: A son should not call his father by his first name, but say "my father, my teacher" or "my honored father."
A common name of others may be mentioned not in the father's presence; a rare name should be altered.
It is permitted to read Scripture mentioning the father's name, and when context clearly shows the father is not meant.
In a signature, "Isaac son of Abraham" is permitted; in a letter or register, write "my honored father."
The same applies regarding one's mother.

mashmaut shel mala kemo vaysimeni leab leparoh veken david hammelek alayv hashshalom qara et shaul hammelek alayv hashshalom beshem abi veken hayu qorin lerab beshem abba bistam "p shehaya shemo iqqere abba vekannizkar besop yoma azel abba lemiqtal veku' veken katab harab rishon letziyyon siman rm"b millat abi moreh al maala gedola kidashkechan beelisha hannabi alayv hashshalom haya qore leeliyyahu zakur lattob abi abi veku' yeuyyan sham ak im kol zeh nahagu lomar abba mari lemala vekabod yoter umatzinu litnay qaddishe dela nahagu bekak deha rabbi yose ben chalapta amar abba chalapta veken rashbi"y amar yochay abba veken oto chakam amar yannay abba venireh dibotam hayyamim lo nahagu beyitron kabod zeh lomar mari ak atta bazzeman hazzeh shennahagu bekak rauy lehizzaher bekak vekatab haggaon chida" za"l deen chilluq bazeh lehaqdim abi al hashshem o lehaqdim hashshem al abi ki ken matzinu gabbe shelomoh hammelek alayv hashshalom paam omer david abi upaam omer abi david yeuyyan sham: vekatabti bsh"q mqbtzyl mah shemmatzinu bimlakim sheamar shelomoh hammelek alayv hashshalom uledavid ulezaro ulebeto ulekiso yihyeh shalom velo amar uledavid abi nireh li dabar zeh amaro betorat tepilla shehiblia tepilla betok debarayv velipne hqb"h haya omer ken bederek tepilla veyadua mah shekkatebu haacharonim za"l dekol shehaadam medabber derek tepilla lipne Adonai en tzorek lomar abi beperush velaken "p sheshshem david haya beoto zeman peliy daadayin lo nitpashshet etzel acherim liqro benehem beshem david dezeh haya samuk liptirato umissetama lo nitpashshet shemo etzel acherim ella achar petirato im kol zeh hu haya mitkavven bidbarim ellu derek tepilla lipne Adonai ulekak en qepida bah umah shemmatzinu beyaaqob abinu alayv hashshalom beparashat vaychi betzavvaato shetztzivva lebanayv sheamar shamma qaberu et abraham et sara ishto shamma qaberu et yitzchaq veet ribqa ishto veshamma qabarti et lea demin hassiyyum shel happasuq mukach dekol happasuq hazzeh hu dibre yaaqob abinu alayv hashshalom velo middibre koteb hattora vetiqshe leka ek mazkir shem yitzchaq veshem ribqa veeno omer abi veimmi vaapillu im nomar shem yitzchaq achar shenniqra bo yitzchaq abinu alayv hashshalom qareu acherim beshem zeh harbeh ubeoto zeman sheddibber bo yaaqob lo haya shem peliy im kol zeh ek yazkir et abiv bishmo apillu achar petirato vaapillu beshem sheeno pile hinneh teratzti bs"d al zeh shekkol debarim hahem shehaya medabber bahem yaaqob abinu alayv hashshalom im banayv haya medabber otam berucha haqqodesh velo hayu debarayv ellu kaasher yedabber im acherim middato uretzono ella rucha haqqodesh shemah bepiv kol haddebarim haelleh ubah haya motzi otam mippiv ulekak hu mukrach lehotzi debarim ellu mippiv betebotehen veotiyyotehen kechepetz uretzon rucha haqqodesh shehaya lah taam kamus benussach zeh velaken hukrach lomar sara ishto veribqa ishto keillu hu medabber al harechoqim mimmennu ukemo shekkatabti kol zeh bsh"q mqbtzyl:

clarification.explanation: Although we said to say "my honored father" or "my father, my teacher" when mentioning his father's name, there is no strict obligation to say "my teacher," and if he said only "my father so-and-so," this suffices, since even the word "my father" carries a meaning of stature and honor, as we find in verses that the term "father" indicates stature. Nevertheless, the custom is to say "my honored father" for additional honor, and it is proper to be careful about this in our time, since this is the custom. There is no difference whether the word "my father" precedes the name or follows it. The halachic conclusion: as the primary practice, one should say "my honored father," though by strict law "my father so-and-so" suffices. The Ben Ish Chai adds a discussion of examples from Scripture: King Solomon sometimes said "David my father" first and sometimes "my father David" — teaching there is no difference in order. And when Solomon said "and for David and his seed and his house and his throne there shall be peace forever" without mentioning "my father," the Ben Ish Chai explains this was said in the language of prayer before God, and just as one speaks in prayer, there is no need to explicitly mention "my father." And regarding our father Jacob, who in his testament to his sons mentioned Sarah and Rebecca as the "wife" of Abraham and Isaac, not saying "my mother" — the Ben Ish Chai explains that Jacob's words there were spoken through the holy spirit, which brought forth from his mouth the words exactly as they needed to be said for a hidden reason, and therefore he spoke of them as though they were distant from him.
takeaways: By strict law, "my father so-and-so" suffices when mentioning the father's name, but the custom adds "my teacher" for extra honor, and one should be careful about this.
There is no difference whether "my father" precedes or follows the father's name.

The Ben Ish Chai resolves apparent difficulties in Scripture about Solomon and Jacob not saying "my father/mother," explaining their words there were spoken in the language of prayer or through the holy spirit.

paragraphs: Ad hekan moraam? haya habben lobesh chamudot veyosheb berosh haqqahal ubau abiv o immo veqareu begadayv vehikkuhu al rosho veyarequ bepinu lo yaklim otam ella yishtoq veyira min melek malke hammelakim hqb"h shetztzivvahu bekak:

clarification.explanation: How far does reverence for parents extend: if the son was dressed in fine garments and sitting at the head of the assembly, and his father or mother came and tore his garments, struck him on the head, and spat in his face, he should not shame them, but remain silent and fear the Holy One, King of kings of kings, who commanded him regarding this.
takeaways: Even if a father or mother humiliate and hurt a son publicly, he should remain silent.
The silence stems from fear of God, who commanded honoring parents.
One should not shame parents even in a severely hurtful situation.

paragraphs: Ezehu kabod maakilo umashqehu malbish umekasseh maknis umotzi veyittenennu lo beseber panim yapot sheapillu maakilo bekol yom petumot vehera lo panim zoapot neenash alayv veken lehepek im matchin abiv berechayim vekavvanato letoba kede sheyyinnatzel abiv middabar qasheh yoter mizzeh umedabber piyyusim al leb abiv umerea lo shekkavvanato letoba ad sheyyirtzeh abiv litchon berechayim hare zeh nochel olam habba vishammeshennu bishar debarim shehashshammash meshammesh et rabbo vehu haddin leimmo kak yaaseh veyitnaheg bekol haddebarim haelleh:

clarification.explanation: What is honoring parents in practice: feeding and giving them drink, clothing and covering them, bringing them in and taking them out, and doing this with a pleasant countenance. Even one who feeds his father delicacies every day but shows him an angry face is punished for it. And conversely: if he burdens his father with hard work but his intent is for his father's own benefit, to save him from something harsher, and speaks to his heart gently, showing him his intent is good until his father agrees, he inherits the World to Come. And he should serve his father in other matters just as a servant serves his master, and behave the same way with his mother.
takeaways: Honor consists of the parents' bodily needs delivered with a pleasant countenance.
An angry face disqualifies even the finest food.
One who burdens his father for his own good, and shows this good intent, inherits the World to Come.

paragraphs: Zeh sheamarnu maakilo umashqehu hen leabiv hen leimmo min mamonam hu kesheyyesh lahem veim en lahem vehabben yesh lo bet din kopin oto lazun abiv veimmo kepi mah shehu yakol abal im en labben mamon kelal sheyyukal lazun otam eno chayyab min haddin lachazor al happetachim kede lehaakil otam veraq nakon laasot ken mitztzad hannimus vederek eretz im epshar lo lachazor al happetachim velo mishshurat haddin mihu chayyab mishshurat haddin lekabbedam begupo "p shemmittok kak batel mimmelakot kol deit leh mazon lehahu yoma debatel mimmelakto abal i let leh mazon lehu yoma eno chayyab mishshurat haddin libbatel mimmelakto hahu yoma velachazor hahu yoma al happachim v"p sheamarnu im yesh lo mishshello kopin oto bet din leparnasatam haynu davqa im yesh lo mazon sheyyaspiq lo lishloshim yom abal im en lo mazon sheyyaspiq lishloshim yom en kopin oto leparnesam mishshello veayyen rishon letziyyon za"l:

clarification.explanation: What we said about a son feeding and giving drink to his parents applies when they have their own money. And if they have none and the son does, the court compels him to support them according to his ability. But if the son has no money at all, he is not obligated by strict law to go door to door to feed them, and it is only proper to do so out of good manners if possible. Nevertheless he is obligated by strict law to honor them with his body, serving them even while foregoing his work, as long as he has food for that day. But if he has no food for the day he would forego his work, he is not obligated by strict law to forego it. And when he is compelled to support them, this is only if he has enough food for thirty days; but if he does not have enough for thirty days, he is not compelled to support them from his own funds.
takeaways: The obligation to feed parents applies to their own money; if they have none and the son is wealthy, the court compels him.
A son is not strictly obligated to beg door to door for his parents, only as a matter of good manners.
He must serve them physically when he has food for the day, but not when he does not.
Compulsion to support them applies only if he has food sufficient for thirty days.

paragraphs: Ab sheyyesh lo banim rabbim mechashshebim bet din hammazon shel ab veem al habbanim lepi mamon shellahem veim miqtzatan ashirin umiqtzatan aniyyim mechayyebin et haashirim bilbad:

clarification.explanation: A father with many sons — the court calculates the expenses for the father's and mother's food and divides them among the sons according to each one's wealth. And if some are wealthy and some poor, only the wealthy are obligated to support the parents.
takeaways: Parental support expenses are divided among the sons according to their wealth.
When there are both wealthy and poor sons, only the wealthy are obligated.

paragraphs: Haya tzarik al shum dabar (hassabbar: dabar kaleshehu) beiro veyodea sheyyeshallemu cheptzo bishbil abiv "p sheyyodea deyaasu gam ken bishbilo lo yomar asu li bishbili ella yomar asu bishbil abba kede litlot hakkabod baabi veen lehaqshot mishshelomoh hammelek alayv hashshalom keshebbiqqesh lehaknis et haaron leqodesh haqqodashim vedibbeqo shearim sheamar techilla al tasheb pene meshicheka velo naana ad sheamar zakera lechasde david abdeka venaana veammay lo amar meiqqara zakera lechasde david abdeka vela hava lah lememar al tasheb pene meshicheka lebaqqesh baaburo dehatam shane dishlomoh hammelek alayv hashshalom yada meiqqara dabar zeh shello dabequ hashshearim ella baabur leharot kebodo shel david hammelek alayv hashshalom abiv ki kebar hibtichahu hqb"h bedabar zeh bechayyayv sheamar lo bechayyeka eni modia ubechay shelomoh binka ani modia ulekak bekavvana mekuvvenet amar techilla esrim vearba renanot veamar al tasheb pene meshicheka sheyyada shello yehi hannaana veen lehaqshot mechizqiyyahu hammelek alayv hashshalom bimlakim b' sheamar anna Adonai zekar na et asher hithallakti lepaneka beemet ubeleb shalem vehattob beeneka asiti velo biqqesh bishbil zekut david hammelek alayv hashshalom vekaasher beemet hqb"h heshib lo aach"k lemaani ulemaan david abdi chada hatam lo haya david abiv veod kol debarim ellu lo neemru ella im medabber habben laacherim kede leharot kebod abiv lipne bene adam abal bidbarim shemmedabber lipne hashshem yitbarak lo shayyak zeh: vekatab harab nachalat tzebi za"l dezeh eno ella beheka dimparesh veomer asu bishbili abal im mebaqqesh en tzarik sheyyomar asu bishbil abba vehebi reaya merabban gamliel bebaqqashato merabbi yehoshua sheamar battechilla mechol li velo amar aseh bishbil abba ella aach"k keshello ratza venireh li deen mizzeh reaya dehatam rabban gamliel hava mistappeq meiqqara im yomar lo aseh bishbil abba yimchol o lav veayyen bashsha"k seip qatan ch' shekkatab im hu mistappeq baddabar hareshut beyado laasot kemo sheyyirtzeh ayyen sham velaken nireh li deim yodea sheyyaasu bishbil abiv apillu mebaqqesh setam tzarik sheyyomar asu bishbil abba veod yesh lemor mehak derabban gamliel en reaya dehatam amar battechilla machul li betorat hodaa sheomer lo ani modeh denaanati leka vetzarik ani lomar leka machul li veaach"k hitchil bedibre baqqasha ubiqqesh techilla bishbil kebod abiv velo bishbil kebodo;

clarification.explanation:
If the son needed something in his city and knows it will be granted for his father's sake, even though he knows it would also be done for his own sake, he should not say "do it for me," but "do it for my father," so as to attribute the honor to his father.

One should not raise a difficulty from King Solomon: when he sought to bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies and the gates stuck, he first said "do not turn away the face of Your anointed" (for his own sake) and was not answered, until he said "remember the mercies of David Your servant" and was answered — why did he not attribute it to his father's honor from the start? The answer is that Solomon knew in advance the gates had stuck only to demonstrate the honor of his father David (as the Holy One had promised even in David's lifetime, "in your lifetime I will not make it known, but in the lifetime of your son Solomon I will make it known"), and therefore he deliberately said it first for his own sake, knowing he would not be answered that way. Nor should one raise a difficulty from King Hezekiah, who said "remember now that I have walked before You in truth" without attributing it to David's merit — since David was not his father, and furthermore this entire law applies only when speaking before people to show his father's honor, but in matters a person speaks before God in prayer, this does not apply at all.

Some say (Nachalat Tzvi) that only if he explicitly says "do it for me" must he correct himself and say "for my father," but if he asks plainly he need not (with proof from Rabban Gamliel, who asked Rabbi Yehoshua "forgive me" first). But the Ben Ish Chai's conclusion is that if he knows it will be done for his father's sake, even asking plainly, he must say "do it for my father."
takeaways: One who knows a request will be granted for his father's sake should say "do it for my father," not "for me," to attribute the honor to him — this applies to matters spoken before people, not before God in prayer.

One should not raise a difficulty from Solomon (who first said "do not turn away Your anointed") — he knew the gates stuck only for David's honor; nor from Hezekiah — David was not his father, and this applies only before people.

Disputed: some say correction is needed only if one explicitly says "for me"; the halachic conclusion (Ben Ish Chai) is that even a plain request requires saying "for my father" if he knows it is for his father's sake.

paragraphs: Chayyab laamod mippene abiv veim haab talmid shel beno zeh omed mippene zeh vezeh omed mippene zeh veim habben rotzeh limchol al kebodo uleshammesh leabiv rashshay derab shemmachal al kebodo kebodo machul vedavqa betzina o apillu beparhesya ak raq beiro shehakkol yodein shehu abiv:

clarification.explanation: A son must stand before his father. And if the father is his son's student, both stand before each other — the father before the son as his teacher, and the son before the father. And if the son wishes to waive his honor and serve his father, he has the authority to, since a teacher who waives his honor, his honor is waived. This is permitted both privately and publicly, but only in the father's own city where everyone knows he is his father.
takeaways: A son must stand before his father.
If the father is the son's student, both stand before each other.
A son may waive his honor to serve his father, but only where it is known he is his father.

paragraphs: Ben haqqam lipne abiv "p sheyyesh lo otah shaa tzorek lelek lo yelek ledarko achar qimato ella yesheb veaach"k yaqum veyelek kede sheyyihyeh nikkar sheqqam lipne abiv velo yihyeh nireh qimato hayeta bishbil lelek ledarko veken hu haddin betalmid asher qam lipne rabbo kaka yaaseh vehu haddin beqima lipne hazzaqen kaasher niktob leqamman mihu im haya lo tzorek otah shaa laasot tzerakayv shennaasa lo hargasha bazeh hen ligdolim hen liqtannim en tzorek lizzaher bekak lesheb achar qimato veaach"k yaqum kede shello yihyeh lo akkaba apillu meat bedabar zeh deit beh issur bal teshaqqetzu veayyen keneset haggedola haggahat hattur ot k':

clarification.explanation: A son who stands before his father, even if he needs to leave at that moment, should not immediately walk away after standing, but should sit down and only afterward rise and leave, so it is clear he stood for his father's honor and does not appear as though he merely stood to leave. The same law applies to a student standing before his teacher and to standing before an elder. But if he needed to relieve himself at that moment and feels this urgently, he need not be careful to sit again, so as not to delay even slightly in a matter carrying the prohibition of "you shall not make yourselves detestable."
takeaways: One who stands for his father should sit again before leaving, so it is clear he stood for his honor.
The same applies to standing before a teacher or an elder.
One needing to relieve himself urgently need not delay, due to "you shall not make yourselves detestable."

paragraphs: Ad hekan kibbud ab vaem apillu natelu kis shel zehubim shello vehishlikuhu layyam lo yaklimem velo yikos kenegdam ella yeqabbel gezerat hakkatub veyishtoq veyesh omerim deim rotzim lizroq maot shel ben layyam yakol lemaneam mihu kol zeh davqa qodem shezzeraqan deepshar demimmani abal im kebar zeraqo asur lehaklimam uledabber kelum kenegdam vegam bazeh davqa heka derotzim laasot lo raq chesron kis abal im rotzim lehaabir mimmennu rivvach bealema asur bekol inyan:

clarification.explanation: How far does honoring one's father and mother extend: even if the parents took a purse full of the son's gold coins and threw it into the sea, he should not shame them or be angry at them, but accept the decree of Scripture and remain silent. Some say that if the parents wish to throw his money into the sea, the son may stop them, but this is only before they throw it, while it can still be prevented; after they have already thrown it, it is forbidden to shame them or say anything to them. And even the permission to stop them applies only when they cause him an actual monetary loss, but if they merely prevent a future profit that would have come, it is forbidden to stop them in any way.
takeaways: Even if parents throw the son's money into the sea, he should not shame or be angry, but remain silent.
It is permitted to stop them before they throw the money, not afterward.
The permission to stop them applies only to an actual monetary loss, not to preventing a future profit.

paragraphs: Chayyab lekabbed et abiv achar moto sheim hu betok y"b chodesh liptirato keshemmazkir shem abiv yomar hareni kapparat mishkabo uleachar y"b chodesh yomar zikrono libraka o alayv hashshalom veim koteb shem abiv bemiktab yesh omerim deen tzarik liktob hareni kapparat mishkabo veyesh machmirin liktob hareni kapparat mishkabo vekol din zeh noheg gam beimmo:

clarification.explanation: A person must honor his father even after his death: within twelve months of his passing, when mentioning his father's name, he should say "I am an atonement for his resting place." After twelve months, he should say "of blessed memory" or "peace be upon him." If he writes his father's name in a letter, some say he need not write "I am an atonement for his resting place," and some are stricter, requiring it. This law applies to one's mother as well.
takeaways: A father is honored even after death, when his name is mentioned.
Within twelve months: "I am an atonement for his resting place"; afterward: "of blessed memory."
The same law applies to one's mother.

paragraphs: Mi shennitrepa daat abiv o immo mishtaddel linhog immahem kepi datam ad sheyyerucham alehem veim i epshar lo laamod mippene shennishtannu beyoter yelek lo veyannichem vitzavveh laacherim lenahagam karauy:

clarification.explanation: One whose father or mother lost their mind and fell ill with a mental illness should try to act toward them according to their perception and condition until God has mercy on them and they are healed. And if he cannot bear this because their mind has changed too greatly, he should go and leave them, instructing others to care for them properly.
takeaways: One whose parents lost their mind should try to accommodate their perception and condition until God has mercy.
If unable to bear it, he should leave and instruct others to care for them properly.

paragraphs: Raa et abiv sheabar al dibre tora lo yomar lo abarta al dibre tora ella yomar lo abba katub battora kak vekak keillu hu shoel mimmennu veeno mazhiro vehu yabin meatzmo velo yitbayyesh vaapillu haya abiv omer shemua betaut lo yomar lo lo titne haki veim abiv am haaretz veraahu abor al dibre tora yomar lepanayv maaseh shehaya beadam echad shekkak vekak asa veamar lo hechakam sheddabar zeh asur denimtza hu mesapper maaseh lepanayv:

clarification.explanation: If a son saw his father transgressing the words of the Torah, he should not tell him explicitly "you transgressed the Torah," but should say to him, "Father, it is written in the Torah thus and so," as though asking him, not in a tone of admonition, and the father will understand on his own without being embarrassed. And even if his father states words of Torah in error, he should not tell him explicitly that he erred. And if his father is an ignoramus and he saw him transgressing the words of Torah, he should relate before him a story about another person who did so, and how a sage told him this thing is forbidden — telling the matter in the manner of a story, not a rebuke.
takeaways: One who sees his father transgressing the Torah should raise it in the tone of a question, not a rebuke.
Even if the father errs in Torah matters, one should not tell him explicitly that he erred.
For an ignorant father, one should raise it through a story about another person.

paragraphs: Amar lo abiv hashqeni mayim o ratza mimmennu tashmish acher leshammesho veyesh lepanayv laasot mitzva oberet kegon qeburat met o levaya vekayyotze im epshar shettaaseh "y acherim hare zeh oseq bikbod abiv veimmo veim lo yaasoq bemitzva veim en hammitzva oberet yaasoq bikbod abiv veaach"k yaaseh hammitzva vegam bemitzva deepshar "y acherim im hitchil bah veaach"k biqqesh abiv mimmennu ezeh eseq yigmor hammitzva veaach"k yaaseh eseq abiv:

clarification.explanation: If his father said to him, "give me water to drink" or asked another service, and the son has before him an active commandment whose time is passing, such as burying the dead or a funeral procession — if the commandment can be performed by others, he should attend to his father's honor; if there is no one else to perform the commandment, he should attend to the commandment. And if the commandment is not time-sensitive and can be done afterward, he should attend first to his father's honor and then to the commandment. And even in a commandment performable by others, if the son already began it and his father then asked him for some service, he should finish the commandment first and then perform his father's request.
takeaways: An active, time-sensitive commandment performable by others yields to a father's honor.
An active commandment with no one else to perform it takes precedence over a father's honor.
A non-time-sensitive commandment yields to a father's honor first; a commandment already begun is finished first.

paragraphs: Amar lo abiv hashqeni mayim veimmo omeret hashqeni mayim mannicha immo veoseq bikbod abiv mippene sheggam immo chayyebet bikbod abiv veim hi megoreshet meabiv shenehem shavim uleezeh mehem sheyyirtzeh yaqdim "g deabiv zakar veyesh lo yitron bechiyyub hammitzot al hanneqeba apillu hake hareshut beyad habben lehaqdim leechad mehem bammeh debarim amurim? im shenehem bachayyim abal im abiv tzivva laasot ezeh dabar veaach"k met veimmo omeret lo laasot hepek yaaseh retzon immo dikbod chay adip:

clarification.explanation: If his father said to him "give me water to drink" and at that same moment his mother said "give me water to drink," he sets aside his mother's request and attends first to his father's honor, since his mother too is obligated in honoring her husband. But if she is divorced from his father, both are equal and the son may prioritize whichever he wishes, even though the father is male and has an advantage in the obligation of commandments. This applies when both are alive, but if his father commanded him to do a certain thing and then died, and his mother asks him to do the opposite, he should do his living mother's will, since honoring the living takes precedence.
takeaways: A father's request takes precedence over a mother's, since she too is obligated to honor her husband.
With divorced parents, both are equal and the son may prioritize whichever he wishes.
A living mother's request takes precedence over a deceased father's earlier command, since honoring the living takes precedence.

paragraphs: Amar lo abiv laabor al dibre tora ben mitzvat aseh ben mitzvat lo taaseh vaapillu mitzva derabbanan lo yishma lo lepikak im tzivva shello yimchol leadam peloni velo yedabber immo vehabben rotzeh laasot shalom immo lo yishma leabiv veken im tzivvahu legaresh et ishto veken shello yaaleh leeretz yisrael lo yishma lo veken amar lo shello yilmad im peloni lo yishma lo veim habben rotzeh lissa ishsha hahogenet lo vechapetz bah - en haab yakol leakkeb veim haya haab rasha ubaal abera apillu hake chayyab habben lekabbedo velihyot lo mora mimmennu veyesh omerim deeno chayyab umikkol maqom asur letzaaro:

clarification.explanation: If his father commanded the son to transgress the words of the Torah, whether a positive commandment, a negative commandment, or even a rabbinic commandment, he should not obey him. Therefore, if he commanded him not to forgive a certain person and not to speak with him, and the son wishes to make peace with him, he should not obey his father. Likewise, if he commanded him to divorce his wife, or not to go up to the Land of Israel, or not to study with so-and-so, he should not obey him. And if the son wishes to marry a woman suitable for him and desires her, the father cannot prevent it. And even if the father is wicked and a transgressor, the son must nevertheless honor him and fear him — though some say he is not obligated — but according to all opinions it is forbidden to cause him distress.
takeaways: A father who commands a transgression, even a rabbinic one, must not be obeyed.
A father cannot prevent forgiveness of others, going up to the Land of Israel, studying with whoever he wishes, or marrying a suitable woman; nor can he force the son to divorce his wife.
Even a wicked father must, according to one view, be honored; according to all opinions, it is forbidden to cause him distress.

paragraphs: Katab bet yosep beshem arechot chayyim en labben lesheb samuk etzel abiv vehebi reaya laddabar ayyen sham, venireh dehaynu davqa bimsibba sheyyesh sham orechim kehak diktib bishmuel ' (k, kh) vayyaqam yehonatan vayyesheb abner mitztzad shaul abal keshehaab bebeto meseb al shulchano im bene beto en qepida bazeh im yashab habben samuk etzel abiv veken haolam en nizharim ella bimsibba shel anashim vezehu davqa bimsibba abal bebet hakkeneset beet hattepilla en qepida abal im niqbatzim laasot vaad yesh qepida bazeh;

clarification.explanation: The Beit Yosef wrote in the name of Orchot Chaim that a son should not sit directly adjacent to his father. Our teacher explains that this applies specifically at a gathering with guests, as we find with Samuel that Jonathan stood while Abner sat beside Saul, but when the father sits at home at his table with his household, there is no concern if the son sits next to him, and so is the common practice, being careful only at a gathering of people. Likewise in the synagogue during prayer there is no concern, but if gathering for a committee meeting, there is concern about this.
takeaways: A son should not sit directly adjacent to his father at a gathering with guests.
At home with household members, there is no concern about sitting next to the father.
In the synagogue during prayer there is no concern, but at a committee gathering there is.

paragraphs: Echad haish veechad haishsha shavin bekabod umora shel ab vaem ella shehaishsha kevan shehi meshubedet lebalah veyesh debarim shel kabod sheen beyadah laasot upetura mehem beodah nesua im balah maqpid veim nitgaresha o nitalmena chayyebet bekol dabar chayyebet bekol dabar:

clarification.explanation: Men and women are equal in the obligation of honoring and revering father and mother. Except that a woman, since she is subordinate to her husband, there are matters of honoring parents she cannot perform, and she is exempt from them while married if her husband insists on this. But if she is divorced or widowed, she is obligated in every matter like any son.
takeaways: Men and women are equal in the obligation to honor and revere parents.
A married woman is exempt from matters of honor her husband insists against.
A divorced or widowed woman is obligated in every matter.

paragraphs: Asur leadam lehakbid ullo al banayv uledaqdeq immahem kede shello yebiem lide mikshol veab shemmachal al kebod kebodo machul vedavqa kebodo abal hakkaato veqillato eno machul veyesh omerim degam tzaar eno machul. v"g demachal al kabod chayyab habben bedine shamayim velaken tzarik laasot tiqqun baabur zeh: vekatub beshaar rucha haqqodesh lerabbenu haari"y za"l tiqqun laabor al matztzat kibbud ab vaem yitanneh esrim veshesh taaniyyot retzupim, veyilqeh kol yom esrim veshesh milleqiyyot vikavven beshem y"h bemilluy alpin kazeh yo"d he" sheppagam bo, ayyen sham vekatabti bs"d "p deday lo tiqqun echad al kamma peamim sheabar bahem al mitzvat kibbud ab vaem mikkol maqom tzarik laasot tiqqun bishbil ab lechud ubishbil em lechud velo day tiqqun echad bishbil shenehem kevan dehem gupim mechullaqim deday lanu lomar desaggi tiqqun echad al maasim mechullaqim mishshum deazelinan batar gup haab. vekatab od beshaar rucha haqqodesh: mi shechata bikbod abiv veimmo - yitanneh chamishsha vearbaim taaniyyot keminyan "ab vaem" (rotzeh lemor im hakkolel) vikavven leshem y"h sheppagam bo. ubeshacharit yekavven leshem y"h bemilluy yvdy"n ubemincha bemilluy lpy"n ubearbit bemilluy hhy"n veod yesh perate kavvanot bah yeuyyan sham vetob shekkol adam yaaseh tiqqun zeh achar petirat abiv veimmo ubenaqel yukal lehitannot taaniyyot ellu veim tash kocho yipdeh otam debar yom beyomo bitzdaqa veyomar baqqasha bepidyon venireh li detiqqun zeh yaspiq bead shenehem:

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden for a person to burden his children with his yoke and be overly exacting with them, so as not to bring them to the stumbling block of disrespect. A father who waives his honor, his honor is waived — but specifically regarding his honor; regarding being struck or cursed, there is no waiver, and some say even regarding causing him distress there is no waiver. And even though he waived his honor, if the son harmed him, he is punished by Heaven's judgment, and therefore a rectification must be performed for this. The Arizal wrote a rectification for one who transgresses the commandments of honoring father and mother: he should fast twenty-six consecutive fasts, and be lashed twenty-six lashes each day, intending the name Yud-Heh in its "alafin" spelling — Yud-Heh — which equals twenty-six, matching the number of fasts and lashes. Our teacher adds that a separate rectification must be done for the father and a separate one for the mother. He further brought a rectification of forty-five fasts, matching the numerical value of "father and mother" with the inclusive count — intending the name Yud-Heh: at morning prayer in its "yudin" spelling, at afternoon prayer in its "alafin" spelling, and at evening prayer in its "heh-hein" spelling; and one whose strength is weakened may redeem them with daily charity, saying a request at the redemption. This rectification suffices for both parents together, unlike the first rectification, which requires a separate one for father and mother. It is good for every person to perform this rectification after his parents' passing.
takeaways: It is forbidden to burden children excessively, lest it lead them to disrespect.
A father waives his own honor, but not being struck, cursed, or (some say) caused distress.
One who harms his father is punished by Heaven even if he waived it, and requires rectification.
The Arizal gave rectifications of fasts and lashes, separate for father and mother, redeemable through charity.

paragraphs: Hammeqallel abiv o immo apillu leachar mita o beshem mehashshemot hamyuchadim chayyab seqila veim qillelam bekinnuy kegon rachum channun chayyab belav kimqallel echad miyyisrael veqatan sheqqillel abiv o immo beqatnuto tzarik kappara begadluto kannizkar beseper chasidim veken meporash bedibre rabbenu haari"y za"l vekol hambazzeh abiv o immo apillu bidbarim vaapillu birmiza hare zeh biklal arur mippi haggebura shenneemar arur maqleh abiv veimmo ubeseper charedim katab shebbiklal zeh im mebazzehu belibbo vehebi maaseh ayyen sham veal zeh yidvu kol kol haddevayyim:

clarification.explanation: One who curses his father or mother, even after their death, using one of God's special names, is liable to death by stoning. If he cursed them using a descriptive term like "Merciful One" or "Gracious One," he is liable for a negative commandment, like one who curses any Jew. A minor who cursed his father or mother in his minority requires atonement when he grows up. And anyone who demeans his father or mother, even in words and even by hinting, falls under the curse stated: "cursed is one who demeans his father and mother." The book Chareidim writes that even one who demeans them in his heart falls under this, and everyone should be greatly distressed about this matter.
takeaways: Cursing parents with God's special name is liable to stoning; with a descriptive term, a negative-commandment liability.
A minor who cursed his parents requires atonement upon reaching adulthood.
Demeaning parents even in words, hinting, or in one's heart falls under the curse.

paragraphs: Ben ish ben ishsha shehikku ab veem veasu bahem chabbura chayyabin cheneq ubehakkaa bilbad beli chabbura chayyabin belav kemo hammakkeh echad miyyisrael velaken im haya qotz tachub leabiv lo yotziennu shemma yaaseh bo chabbura vehu haddin leimmo veken im ben umman lehaqqiz dam lo yaqqiz leabiv o leimmo bammeh debarim amurim? kesheyyesh acher laasot lahem abal im en acher laasot umitztaarim hare zeh maqqiz veoseh kol mah sheyyarshuhu laasot lahem:

clarification.explanation: Whether a man or a woman who struck their father or mother and caused a wound (an injury from which blood emerged) is liable to death by strangulation, and for striking alone without a wound, liable for a negative commandment, like one who strikes any Jew. Therefore, if a thorn was stuck in his father, the son should not remove it, lest he cause a wound, and likewise regarding his mother. Likewise, if the son is a professional bloodletter, he should not perform bloodletting on his father or mother. This applies when there is another person who can do it, but if there is no one else and the parents are suffering, the son may perform bloodletting and do everything they have permitted him to do to them.
takeaways: Striking a parent and causing a wound is liable to strangulation; without a wound, a negative-commandment liability.
A son should not remove a thorn from a parent or perform bloodletting on them, lest he cause a wound.
When no one else is available and the parents are suffering, the son may do so with their permission.

paragraphs: Asur labben limchol al kebod abotayv velaabor al middotayv bemilleta deabuha veimmeh mitztaarim vekannizkar bikneset haggedola uben sheyyodea sheabiv veimmo mitztaarim al shehu mitanneh lo yitanneh betaanit sheenam choba vekannizkar beseper chasidim:

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden for a son to waive his ancestors' honor and transgress their customs and practices in a matter that distresses his father and mother. And a son who knows that his father and mother are distressed by his fasting should not observe a voluntary, non-obligatory fast.
takeaways: A son may not waive his parents' honor by transgressing their customs in a matter that distresses them.
A son whose parents are distressed by his fasting should not observe a voluntary fast.

paragraphs: Im haem tzivveta libnah laasot dabar deshoel haab mi amar leka shettaaseh dabar zeh im yodea sheabiv yikos aleha viqallelenna lo yomar lo sheimmo tzivveta vekannizkar sham:

clarification.explanation: If the mother instructed her son to do something, and the father asks him "who told you to do this," if the son knows his father will become angry at his mother and curse her, he should not tell him that his mother instructed him, so as not to cause a quarrel and cursing.
takeaways: If the mother instructed and the father asks who instructed, the son should not reveal that it was the mother.
The reason: to avoid causing the father to become angry and curse the mother.

paragraphs: Bemaqom shennahagu liqrot ben hannolad rishon al shem abiv, veimmo rotza liqroto al shem abiha, lo yukal habbaal laasot retzon ishto bedabar zeh ella tzarik lehaqdim liqro bo harishon al shem abiv vehashsheni yiqraennu al shem abiha. upuq chazi may saleq benadab vaabihu mippene sheqqara ben harishon al shem abi ishto, vekannizkar bisdeh haaretz cheleq g' siman k"b. vekatab beiqqere hd"t sheim yirtzeh liqrot habben al shem shenehem yaqdim shem abiv:

clarification.explanation: In a place where the custom is to name the firstborn son after the father's father, and the mother wishes to name him after her own father, the husband cannot fulfill his wife's wish in this, but must first name the first son after his own father, and the second son after the wife's father. See what happened with Nadav, the firstborn son, whom Aaron named after his wife's father. It is written in Ikarei HaDinim that if one wishes to name a son after both grandfathers, he should place the father's father's name first.
takeaways: Where the custom prevails, the firstborn is named after the father's father, not the mother's father.
The second son may be named after the mother's father.
One wishing to combine both grandfathers' names should place the father's father's name first.

paragraphs: Chayyab lekabbed eshet abiv kol zeman sheabiv qayyam v"p sheimmo maqpedet diktib kabbed et abika lerabbot eshet abika veken chayyab lekabbed al immo "p sheabiv maqpid ukegon sheggereshah abiv venisset leacher diktib et immeka lerabbot al immeka vegam zeh hu kol zeman sheimmo qayyemet abal leachar mita eno chayyab umikkol maqom debar hagun hu lekabbedam ap leachar mita:

clarification.explanation: A person must honor his father's wife as long as his father is alive, even if his own mother objects, as it is said, "honor your father" to include your father's wife. Likewise he must honor his mother's husband when his father divorced her and she remarried another, even if his father objects, as it is said, "your mother" to include your mother's husband — and this applies as long as his mother is alive. But after the parents' death, he is not obligated in their honor, though it is nevertheless proper conduct to honor them even after death.
takeaways: One must honor his father's wife while his father is alive, even if his own mother objects.
One must honor his divorced mother's new husband while his mother is alive, even if his father objects.
After the parents' death there is no obligation, though it is proper to honor them still.

paragraphs: Chayyab adam bikbod achiv haggadol ben shehu achiv meabiv ben achiv meimmo vaapillu haqqatan hu talmid chakam vegadol battora yoter min haggadol gam ken chayyab bikbodo veken hashshelishi chayyab bikbod hashsheni veken al zeh hadderek velav davqa hazzekarim ella gam achyotayv hanneqebot shehem gedolim mimmennu chayyab lekabbedam ukemo shekkatab rabbenu haari"y za"l beshaar taame hammitzot:

clarification.explanation: A person is obligated in honoring his older brother, whether a brother from the father's side or the mother's side. And even if the younger brother is a greater Torah scholar than the older brother, the younger is obligated in honoring the older. Likewise the third brother is obligated in honoring the second, and so on. And not only male brothers, but he is also obligated to honor his older sisters.
takeaways: A person is obligated in honoring his older brother, whether paternal or maternal.
Even a younger brother greater in Torah scholarship is obligated in honoring the older.
The obligation applies also toward older sisters.

paragraphs: Chayyab bikbod chamiv velaken david hammelek alayv hashshalom qara et shaul hammelek alayv hashshalom, "abi raa gam raa" (shemuel  kd, yb) vehu haddin dechayyab bikbod chamoto veken haishsha chayyebet lekabbed chamiha vachamotah vekatab beshiyyure beraka beshem tanna debe eliyyahu sheim nasa ishsha veenah mekabbedet abiv veimmo leet ziqnatan hare hu keillu noep kol yamayv lekak dibbur lo tinap samuk ledibbur kabbed et abika veet immeka yeuyyan sham vechayyab adam bikbod abi abiv veken beem abiv vehu haddin dechayyab bikbod abi immo vechayyab name lekabbed achi abiv vaachi immo vealayv tabo birkat tob:

clarification.explanation: A person is obligated in honoring his father-in-law, and therefore King David called King Saul, his father-in-law, using the term "my father, look and see." Likewise he is obligated in honoring his mother-in-law, and a wife is obligated to honor her father-in-law and mother-in-law. It is written in the name of Tanna DeBei Eliyahu that one who marries a woman who does not honor his parents in their old age is considered as though he commits adultery all his days, and therefore the commandment "you shall not commit adultery" is placed next to the commandment "honor your father and mother." A person is also obligated in honoring his paternal grandfather and grandmother, and likewise his maternal grandfather, and is likewise obligated to honor his paternal and maternal uncles, and blessing will come upon him.
takeaways: A person is obligated in honoring his father-in-law and mother-in-law, and a wife likewise toward her in-laws.
One who marries a woman who does not honor his parents in their old age is considered as committing adultery all his days.
A person is also obligated in honoring his grandparents and his paternal and maternal uncles.
